verses.text: That day King Ahasuerus gave Queen Esther the estate of Haman, the enemy of the Jews. Mordecai came before the king because Esther had told him how they were related.
The king took off the signet ring he'd taken back from Haman and gave it to Mordecai. Esther put Mordecai in charge of Haman's estate.
Esther spoke to the king again. She fell at his feet and begged him through tears to stop the harm Haman the Agagite had plotted against the Jews.
The king held out the gold scepter to Esther, so she got up and stood before him.

She said, "If it pleases the king, if I've found favor with him, and if this seems right to him and he is pleased with me, let an order be written reversing the letters Haman son of Hammedatha the Agagite wrote to destroy the Jews in all the royal provinces.
How can I bear to see disaster come upon my people? How can I bear to watch my own family be destroyed?"
King Ahasuerus told Queen Esther and Mordecai the Jew, "I've given Esther Haman's estate, and he was hanged because he attacked the Jews.
Write whatever you think best for the Jews in the king's name and seal it with the king's ring. No one can revoke a document written in the king's name and sealed with his ring."

The royal scribes were called on the twenty-third day of the third month, Sivan. They wrote everything Mordecai ordered for the Jews and for the governors and officials of the hundred twenty-seven provinces from India to Ethiopia. They used each province's script and each people's language, including the script and language of the Jews.
Mordecai wrote in King Ahasuerus's name and sealed the letters with the king's ring. He sent them out with couriers riding fast horses bred for royal service.

The letters granted the Jews in every city the right to gather and defend their lives. They could destroy any armed force from any people or province that attacked them, their children, or their women, and take their attackers' possessions.
This permission was for one day throughout King Ahasuerus's provinces, the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, Adar.
A copy of the order was made public to all peoples in each province so the Jews could be ready that day to take vengeance on their enemies.
At the king's urgent command, the couriers rode out quickly on royal horses. The decree was also announced in the fortress of Susa.
Mordecai left the king's presence wearing blue and white royal robes, a large gold crown, and a robe of fine linen and purple cloth. The city of Susa shouted with joy.
For the Jews there was light, gladness, joy, and honor.
In every province and city where the king's decree arrived, the Jews celebrated with joy, feasting, and a holiday. Many people of the land became Jews because fear of the Jews had come over them.
